title: A Microfluidic Chip for ICPMS Sample Introduction
protocol: Dehydrate a silicon wafer for 10 min at 200 °C.
Cool the wafer down to room temperature and load it onto a spin coater.
Spin coat the wafer with SU-8 2002: dispense about 3 ml resist onto the wafer.
Spin the wafer at 500 rpm for 10 sec.
Spin the wafer at 2,000 rpm for 30 sec to achieve a resist height of approximately 2 µm.
Remove excess resist from the edge of the wafer with an acetone-soaked swab.
Bake the wafer for 60 sec at 95 °C on a hot plate.
Expose the whole wafer with ultraviolet light (80 mJ/cm² at 365 nm).
Post-bake the wafer for 120 sec to 95 °C.
Cool the wafer down and immediately spin coat the wafer again using SU-8 2050: spin the wafer at 100 rpm for 20 sec (dispense about 3 ml SU-8 resist during this step).
Spin the wafer at 500 rpm for 10 sec to spread the resist over the whole wafer.
Spin the wafer at 3,250 rpm for 30 seconds.
Remove excess resist from the edge of the wafer with an acetone-soaked swab.
Soft bake the wafer on a hot plate for 180 seconds at 65°C.
Soft bake the wafer on a hot plate for 360 seconds at 95°C.
Stick the photomask to soda-lime glass.
Expose the resist with ultraviolet light (160 mJ/cm²) through the prepared mask using a mask aligner.
Bake the exposed wafer again on a hot plate for 60 seconds at 65°C.
Bake the exposed wafer again on a hot plate for 360 seconds at 95°C.
Immerse the cooled wafer in a glass Petri dish filled with developer for 5 minutes to develop the resist.
Gently agitate the Petri dish to remove unexposed SU-8.
Rinse the wafer with isopropanol.
Blow dry the wafer with a nitrogen gun.
Examine the wafer under a microscope.
Develop the wafer again if undeveloped resist remains on the features, for several minutes as described in step 1.7.
Bake the wafers for 2 hours at 200°C to remove any residual solvent.
Check the height of the features with a step profiler.
Begin the protocol again and adapt the spin speed in step 1.1.4 if the measured height differs from the desired height.
Silanize the wafer by placing it in a desiccator together with 50 µl of 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorodecyltrichlorosilane in a small porcelain dish.
Reduce the pressure in the desiccator to 100 mbar.
Incubate the wafer for 12 hours.
Silanize another silicon wafer using the method from step 1.10.
Mix 40 g of prepolymer with 4 g of PDMS curing agent to prepare 44 g of PDMS.
Degas the PDMS in a desiccator until it is bubble free, which takes about 20 minutes.
Pour approximately 3 to 4 g of degassed PDMS into the casting form.
Place the casting form on top of the wafer and snap it into place using guiding structures around the design.
Heat the casting form with PDMS on a hot plate at 150 °C for 6 minutes.
Cool down the cured PDMS in the casting form.
Carefully lift the casting form off the wafer using a spatula.
Cover the side of the chip that was previously in contact with the wafer with tape to prevent contamination of microfluidic channels.
Carefully cut the tape along the edge of the PDMS part to remove excess PDMS.
Spin coat an untreated silicon wafer with PDMS curing agent for 30 seconds at 6,000 rpm.
Remove the tape from the structured halves and place them structures facing downwards onto the coated wafer.
Gently push on top of the PDMS to remove air bubbles.
Remove the tape from the blank PDMS halves.
Manually align a structured half on top of the flat PDMS halve.
Gently squeeze the parts together to remove air bubbles, then let the assembled chip cure for 24 hours at room temperature.
Cut the tip of the chip along the indicator line orthogonal to the nozzle channel with a utility knife.
Inspect the chip under a microscope for defects in the microfluidic channels and dust particles.
Put a tape over the inlet holes to protect the chips during storage.
Connect a Woulff bottle with tubing to a dry nitrogen source and all inlets of the LADE chip.
Deposit 50 μl of 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorodecyltrichlorosilane at the bottom of the Woulff bottle.
Close the Woulff bottle.
Silanize the microfluidic channels by flushing all channels for 20 min with a nitrogen stream carrying 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorodecyltrichlorosilane at a flow rate of approximately 1 ml/sec.
Install a custom cyclonic poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) adapter with an attached stainless steel tube vertically.
Attach the PMMA adapter to a helium source with a mass flow controller.
Attach a high-speed camera and a lamp to the adapter on opposite sides for droplet visualization.
Place a cartridge heater in the middle of the steel tube.
Connect the end of the steel tube with the inlet of the membrane desolvator using PVC tubing and a Legris tube connector.
Connect the outlet of the desolvator with another PVC tubing to a laminar flow adapter.
Directly connect the laminar flow adapter to the ICPMS inlet.
Connect the laminar flow adapter to an argon source using a mass flow controller.
Insert a plug into the adapter to prevent gas leaks during warm-up.
Start all gas flows and devices according to settings in Table 1.
Allow the system to warm up for 15 minutes.
Switch on the cartridge heater at least 2 hours before use.
Place syringe pumps on a rack at the height of the cyclonic helium adapter.
Keep the distance between syringe pumps and adapter as short as possible.
Attach tubing to the syringes.
Load two 5 ml syringes with perfluorohexane.
Load one 1 ml syringe with a sample solution or suspension.
Remove bubbles trapped in the syringes and tubing.
Install the syringes in a syringe pump.
Connect the syringes to the chip's inlets.
Start the syringe pumps using settings from Table 1 (or higher flow rates).
Give the flows 3 to 5 min to stabilize.
Remove excess liquid from the tip of the chip with a tissue.
Replace the chip and start over if straight ejection cannot be achieved by wiping.
Insert the chip into the adapter after removing the plug.
Lubricate the chip with FC-40 if necessary.
Change flow rates within recommended measurement settings from Table 1.
Give the system 2 to 5 min to stabilize depending on chosen flow rates.
Optimize ICPMS for highest signal intensity of analytes of interest.
Adjust flows of all gases on mass flow controllers until maximum signal is achieved.
Tune plasma power and focusing lens voltages according to manufacturer's recommended ranges.
Set the ICPMS dwell time to 10 msec.
Start recording the signal of a particular m/z using manufacturer’s protocol.
Transfer raw data to data analysis program for evaluation.
Bin data, given in counts per 10 msec, with built-in function.
Plot resulting bin center values against counts.
Fit each peak in the plotted frequency distribution histogram with a Gauss function.
Measure a single or multi-element standard solution containing the element or elements of interest at the same flow rates as the sample.
Place a LADE chip in a petri dish on a microscope.
Use a non-round chip for better image quality.
Fabricate this chip using a simple rectangular casting form.
Follow steps 4.1 to 4.2.1 to start droplet generation.
Set the flow rates to those used in step 5.1.
Record images of aqueous droplets with a high-speed camera attached to a microscope using a 20X objective.
Use an image analysis software like the droplet morphometry and velocimetry software by Basu to obtain the average droplet diameter from the recordings.
Calculate the droplet volume assuming the droplet is a spherical object.
From this volume, calculate the number of corresponding atoms given the known concentration of an analyte in the droplet.
Divide the number of measured ions per droplet by the number of atoms to obtain the detection efficiency.
Use this detection efficiency to calculate the number of atoms in an unknown sample.
